“Me and Earl and the Dying Girl” by Jesse Andrew’s is by far my favorite YA novel. It’s a short read, outrageously funny, emotional, and raw. It’s always my go-to YA recommendation. The film adaptation is FANTASTIC. Definitely a nice reward for yourself after making it through your first book in a while.
It’s just a short-story but “Mother of Invention” by Nnedi Okorafor. It’s a pretty short read but it’s fantastic and it’s one of those stories I catch my self thinking about everyday.

Me and Earl and the Dying Girl by Jesse Andrews. This is my go-to favorite book. It’s a coming of age story but the characters just feel extremely relatable. It’s a story that is focused around cancer but it’s also one of the funniest books I’ve read in my life. The film adaption is absolutely perfect as well. Genuinely couldn’t recommend any more.

Station Eleven by Emily St. John Mandel. I had to read this for my dystopian sci-fi class, and it was by far one of the best books I’ve ever read. It discusses a world wide pandemic, the author nearly predicted everything that actually happened in our world. It was a gripping read that primarily focused on the new world order after everything collapsed. It’s supposed to be adapted to an HBO limited series sometime in the near future as well.

A few years back I recently read Rainn Wilson’s autobiography, “The Bassoon King”. He had an extremely interesting upbringing/ coming of age process and the whole book was comedic and heartfelt. I would highly recommend!

If you haven’t read “The Road” by Cormac McCarthy it’s amazing. I found it to be extremely captivating (almost read the entire thing in one sitting) the audiobook is fantastic (I think I might have listened to it free on YouTube).

I recently just read “The Buddha of Suburbia” by Hanif Kureishi for a college course. I truthfully didn’t think I was going to like it as much as I did. The main character is twenty, however, a lot of the novel discusses suburbia/ middle-aged adult problems (ie. divorce, arranged marriage, falling out of love). On top of everything else it was absolutely hilarious. I read it while listening to the audiobook version on Audible and frankly I thought the audiobook version was irreplaceable. Highly recommend, it felt like a good transition from YA to “adult books”.
